rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + Hx of epistaxis since adolescence + they show you pic of a tongue with a red dot on it + dyspnea + high ejection fraction (75-80%); Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on NBME = pulmonary arteriovenous malformation → presentation is hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu) → USMLE will always show you a red dot on the tongue or fingernail → Q may also mention fatigue (GI bleeding) → autosomal dominant.

rapidFireQAs.q: Postmenopausal woman + stress factor + bulging of LV on echo + hypercontractile LV base; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy → “ballooning of LV” → once again, weird Dx but USMLE likes it.

rapidFireQAs.q: Atherosclerosis; where does the process start?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE answer = endothelial cell, not adipocyte.

rapidFireQAs.q: Congenital heart block; Dx in the mom?
rapidFireQAs.a: SLE → 1-5% of SLE mothers will have kid with CHB.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate with supravalvular aortic stenosis; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: kid has William syndrome (chromosome 7, AD; elfin-like facies; hypercalcemia due to increased vitamin D sensitivity; well-developed verbal skills).

rapidFireQAs.q: Left ventricular hypertrophy; USMLE asks arrow Q
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = transcription factor c-Jun activity is increased; beta-myosin heavy chain gene expression is increased; endothelin is increased.

rapidFireQAs.q: 65M + 2-3-day Hx of severe chest pain + dyspnea + visible pulsation above manubrium + tracheal deviation + murmur in 2nd intercostal space on the right; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE answer = aortic aneurysm.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dysphagia and/or hoarseness caused by dilated cardiac structure; which structure is dilated?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = left atrium → the hoarseness is due to recurrent laryngeal nerve impingement by LA (Ortner syndrome).

rapidFireQAs.q: Location of SA node?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on NBME = “junction of superior vena cava and right atrium.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Location of AV node?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer on NBME = “inferior to the opening of the coronary sinus” → it is located on the posteroinferior interatrial septum near the coronary sinus.

rapidFireQAs.q: Location of coronary sinus?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = “between the opening of the IVC and the tricuspid valve.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate with truncus arteriosus; Q is which of the following populations of cells was most likely absent during cardiac development?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE answer = “ectodermal neural crest” cells.

rapidFireQAs.q: Fetal alcohol syndrome + heart/lung fistula; mechanism?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = “failure of migration of neural crest cells.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of death due to fall or MVA?
rapidFireQAs.a: traumatic rupture of the aorta (thoracic).

rapidFireQAs.q: Where does rupture of the aorta occur?
rapidFireQAs.a: where the ligamentum arteriosum wraps around the top of the descending arch → ligament is taut but arch is more mobile → leads to shearing.

rapidFireQAs.q: What will the NBME/USMLE Q say for traumatic rupture
rapidFireQAs.a: MVA or fall followed by “widening of the mediastinum on CXR.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for traumatic rupture?
rapidFireQAs.a: if ascending arch: labetalol + surgery; if descending arch: labetalol only.

rapidFireQAs.q: BP different between the arms; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: aortic dissection or subclavian steal syndrome.

rapidFireQAs.q: Most likely cause of dissection?
rapidFireQAs.a: HTN, but connective tissue disorders (e.g., Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, MYH11 mutations) also important.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for dissection?
rapidFireQAs.a: if ascending aortic arch, answer = labetalol + surgery; if descending arch, answer = labetalol only (HY, since everyone chooses surgery) → do not choose sodium nitroprusside here.

rapidFireQAs.q: High TGAs + high chylomicrons on lab report; Dx + mechanism?
rapidFireQAs.a: familial hyperchylomicronemia; answer on USMLE = “deficiency of apolipoprotein C-II” or “deficiency of lipoprotein lipase.”

rapidFireQAs.q: Normal TGAs + high LDL on lab report; Dx + mechanism?
rapidFireQAs.a: familial hypercholesterolemia; answer on USMLE = “deficiency of LDL receptor.” If total cholesterol is ~3-500s mg/dL, USMLE wants “deficiency”; if total is ~700-1000 mg/dL, the answer = “absence of functional LDL receptors on hepatocytes.”

rapidFireQAs.q: High TGAs + normal LDL on lab report; Dx + mechanism?
rapidFireQAs.a: familial hypertriglyceridemia; answer on USMLE = “increased hepatic production of VLDL.”

rapidFireQAs.q: “Creamy plasma” on laboratory inspection. Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: familial hyperchylomicronemia.

rapidFireQAs.q: Confused old man + temp of 96F + CO high + PCWP low + TPR low; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: septic shock → dementia increases risk of aspiration pneumonia due to diminished gag reflex (important cause of sepsis) → by all means the vignette might say urinary retention in BPH, or tell you there’s a catheter → also important causes of sepsis here.

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient with infective endocarditis + now has limb weakness or sensory findings; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: septic embolus → answer = give immediate IV antibiotics.

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient with alternating tachycardia + bradycardia; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: sick sinus syndrome → caused by damage to SA node (i.e., due to coronary artery or valvular disease, or autoimmunity, e.g., sarcoidosis) → Tx with atrial pacemaker.

rapidFireQAs.q: Diffuse ST-segment elevations on ECG; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pericarditis.

rapidFireQAs.q: If infective, most likely etiology of pericarditis? (answers are bacteria, parasitic, fungal, etc.); answer = viral
rapidFireQAs.a: viruses can cause serous pericarditis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M after night of heavy partying + central chest pain worse when leaning back + better when leaning forward; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: serous pericarditis caused by cocaine.

rapidFireQAs.q: 68F diabetic + high K + high BUN + high Cr + friction rub in central chest; Dx + Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: uremic pericarditis → answer on USMLE = immediate hemodialysis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + had STEMI two days ago + now has central friction rub; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: post-MI fibrinous pericarditis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 72M + had STEMI 2-6 weeks ago + now has central friction rub; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: Dressler syndrome (autoantibodies causing fibrinous pericarditis).

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + ulnar deviation + MCP/PIP pain + heart problem; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pericarditis → autoimmune diseases like RA and SLE cause serous pericarditis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 34F + anti-Scl70 (topoisomerase I) Abs + heart issue; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: pericardial fibrosis due to systemic sclerosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: High-Yield Pearl #36
rapidFireQAs.a: Kid + heart tumor = cardiac rhabdomyoma until proven otherwise (usually tuberous sclerosis).

rapidFireQAs.q: Adult + heart tumor = cardiac myxoma until proven otherwise (ball-in-valve tumor in the left atrium
rapidFireQAs.a: causes murmur that abates when patient is positioned in an unusual way, e.g., on his right side while leaning diagonally).

rapidFireQAs.q: 2-year-old boy has cardiac myxoma (correct, not rhabdomyoma) + perioral melanosis (sophisticated way of saying hyperpigmentation around the mouth/lips) + hyperthyroidism; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = Carney complex → this is asked on the USMLE → classically triad of cardiac myxoma + perioral melanosis + endocrine hypersecretion (classically bilateral pigmented zona fasciculata hyperplasia resulting Cushing syndrome, but can be hyperthyroidism or growth hormone).

rapidFireQAs.q: What does S1 heart sound mean?
rapidFireQAs.a: closure of atrioventricular valves (mitral + tricuspid), signifying onset of systole.

rapidFireQAs.q: What does S2 heart sound mean?
rapidFireQAs.a: closure of semilunar valves (aortic + pulmonic), signifying onset of diastole.

rapidFireQAs.q: What does S3 heart sound mean?
rapidFireQAs.a: early-diastolic reverberation caused by dilated left ventricle → often synonymous with dilated cardiomyopathy on the USMLE; yes, it can be seen sometimes incidentally in pregnancy and young athletes (due to increased preload), but almost always it just means dilated cardiomyopathy.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is a parasternal heave?
rapidFireQAs.a: a parasternal heave means the heartbeat can be felt (or sometimes seen) along the left sternal border, usually due to RVH (since the RV is most anterior) → RVH can be seen in ventricular septal defect (VSD), so parasternal heave can be seen in VSD.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is a palpable thrill?
rapidFireQAs.a: a palpable thrill is merely a palpable murmur; it carries no additional diagnostic significance; a thrill is seen in grades 4-6 of the heart sounds.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the 6 grades of heart sounds? (not asked on USMLE, but just for your own knowledge with respect to this document)
rapidFireQAs.a: 1: very faint; not heard in all positions (“cardiologist only”); 2: faint; heard in all positions; 3: loud, with no thrill; 4: loud with palpable thrill; 5: loud with palpable thrill + can be heard with stethoscope partially off chest; 6: loud with palpable thrill + can be heard with the stethoscope completely off the chest.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which murmurs are holosystolic (aka pansystolic)?
rapidFireQAs.a: mitral regurgitation (mitral insufficiency; MR) + tricuspid regurgitation (tricuspid insufficiency; TR); ventricular septal defect (VSD).

rapidFireQAs.q: Which murmurs are mid-systolic (crescendo-decrescendo systolic)?
rapidFireQAs.a: aortic stenosis (AS) + hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) + pulmonic stenosis (PS).

rapidFireQAs.q: Which murmur has a diastolic opening snap?
rapidFireQAs.a: mitral stenosis (MS) → has diastolic opening snap, followed by a mid-late decrescendo diastolic murmur.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which murmur has a mid-systolic click?
rapidFireQAs.a: mitral valve prolapse (MVP).

rapidFireQAs.q: Which murmur can also be described as a late-peaking systolic murmur with an ejection click?
rapidFireQAs.a: AS.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which murmur is continuous machinery-like?
rapidFireQAs.a: patent ductus arteriosus (PDA); can also be AV fistulae.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which murmur is pansystolic-pandiastolic?
rapidFireQAs.a: PDA (same as continuous machinery-like).

rapidFireQAs.q: Which murmur is to-and-fro?
rapidFireQAs.a: PDA; same as continuous or pansystolic-pandiastolic.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which murmur is fixed splitting of S2?
rapidFireQAs.a: atrial septal defect (ASD).

rapidFireQAs.q: Which murmurs are holodiastolic (pandiastolic)?
rapidFireQAs.a: aortic regurgitation (aortic insufficiency; AR) + pulmonic regurgitation (pulmonic insufficiency; PR).

rapidFireQAs.q: Which murmur is pandiastolic and loudest in early-diastole?
rapidFireQAs.a: classically AR (decrescendo holodiastolic murmur).

rapidFireQAs.q: Young child + hypocalcemia + harsh systolic murmur at left sternal border; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: DiGeorge syndrome associated with tetralogy of Fallot → on the USMLE, you should essentially think of ToF and DiGeorge syndrome as interchangeable → you can by all means get other heart defects in DiGeorge, e.g., truncus arteriosus, but I can’t emphasize enough that ToF is almost always seen in DiGeorge on USMLE.

rapidFireQAs.q: How do the heart murmurs change with volume in the heart (i.e., do they get louder/softer with more/less volume)?
rapidFireQAs.a: all will get worse / more prominent with more volume in the heart, however MVP and HOCM are the odd ones out; they’ll get worse with less volume in the heart. No change = softer on USMLE. So for example, AS will be no change or softer with Valsalva. Valsalva decreases volume in the heart.

rapidFireQAs.q: 8F + sickle cell + fever + HR of 120 + normal BP + 2/6 mid-systolic murmur at upper right sternal border; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: transient, functional high-flow murmur secondary to tachycardia → called functional because murmur will subside once HR returns to baseline.

rapidFireQAs.q: 13F + Hb of 7 g/dL + HR of 120 + normal BP + 2/6 mid-systolic murmur at upper right sternal border; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: once again, transient, functional flow murmur → I point this out because students often erroneously think there’s some heart abnormality when they see this type of murmur.

rapidFireQAs.q: Aortic stenosis (AS) – what will you auscultate?
rapidFireQAs.a: mid-systolic (crescendo-decrescendo systolic) murmur classically at 2nd intercostal space, right sternal border, with radiation to the carotids; however will also show up as “late-peaking systolic murmur with an ejection click.” → don’t confuse the latter with “mid-systolic click,” which is mitral valve prolapse (MVP).

rapidFireQAs.q: Who gets AS?
rapidFireQAs.a: classically bicuspid aortic valve → can be familial autosomal dominant; also seen in Turner syndrome (45XO) → leads to early calcification of valve in the 40s onward; however a young patient without significant calcification can easily have AS. USMLE gives Qs of children with bicuspid aortic valve and aortic stenosis and students are somehow surprised by this ("I thought it had to be adults though.")

rapidFireQAs.q: What about if the patient doesn’t have bicuspid valve?
rapidFireQAs.a: AS can still occur in the general population with normal senile calcification seen typically age 70s-80s onward (i.e., incidental 1/6 or 2/6 mid-systolic murmur in otherwise healthy elderly patient).

rapidFireQAs.q: How does AS classically present Sx-wise?
rapidFireQAs.a: SAD → Syncope, Angina, Dyspnea.

rapidFireQAs.q: AS causes what kind of LVH?
rapidFireQAs.a: concentric hypertrophy due to pressure overload → can also cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with an S4 heart sound (stiff LV). This is in contrast to aortic regurgitation (aortic insufficiency), which causes eccentric hypertrophy due to volume overload.

rapidFireQAs.q: What kind of pulse is seen in AS?
rapidFireQAs.a: slow-rising pulse (“pulsus parvus et tardus”). Don’t confuse this with AR, which causes bounding pulses with head-bobbing (Q will often say for AR: “pulse has brisk upstroke with precipitous downstroke.”).

rapidFireQAs.q: Any weird factoid about AS?
rapidFireQAs.a: Heyde syndrome is the combo of AS + angiodysplasia (painless rectal bleeding in elderly due to superficial tortuous vessels on the bowel wall) → shows up on NBME.

rapidFireQAs.q: What does HOCM sound like?
rapidFireQAs.a: same as AS (mid-systolic murmur, aka crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur).

rapidFireQAs.q: What causes HOCM?
rapidFireQAs.a: autosomal dominant mutation in beta-myosin heavy-chain gene.

rapidFireQAs.q: What’s the structural change in the heart with HOCM?
rapidFireQAs.a: asymmetric septal hypertrophy that causes the anterior mitral valve leaflet to block off the LV outflow tract under states of lesser preload → student says, “if the LV outflow tract is blocked off (i.e., where the aortic valve is), why is it the mitral valve leaflet that blocks it off then?” Yeah, I know, it’s weird. But the asymmetric septal hypertrophy causes this to happen.

rapidFireQAs.q: What’s the cause of death in HOCM?
rapidFireQAs.a: ventricular fibrillation due to acute left-heart strain → the “sudden death in young athlete” is not due to an MI → i.e., the patient has clean coronary arteries → do not select coronary artery occlusion as the answer.

rapidFireQAs.q: What about if the vignette is sudden death in middle-aged patient with heart disease?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = ischemic heart disease (MI), not HOCM.

rapidFireQAs.q: 18M athlete + 2/6 mid-systolic murmur at right sternal border 2nd intercostal space + there is paradoxical splitting of S2 + there is no change in the murmur with Valsalva; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: ”bicuspid aortic valve” (AS), not HOCM → students say “oh em gee young athlete! HOCM!” → the USMLE will slam you on this and wants you to know that the key way to distinguish between AS and HOCM murmurs is that HOCM gets worse with lower volume in the heart; AS will soften or there will be no change. Don’t just automatically jump on HOCM because it’s a young athlete.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Tx HOCM
rapidFireQAs.a: can give propranolol to keep HR from getting too fast (the slower the HR, the more time the heart spends in diastole → more diastolic filling → greater preload → less occlusion of LV outflow tract) → should be noted tangentially that although beta-blockers increase preload, they decrease chronotropy + inotropy so the net effect is still decreased myocardial oxygen demand.

rapidFireQAs.q: Can you explain “splitting of S2”? What does that even mean?
rapidFireQAs.a: the aortic valve normally shuts (A2) just before the pulmonic valve (P2), so A2 will occur slightly before P2 → when we talk about changes in splitting of the S2 heart sound (i.e., wide splitting, paradoxical splitting, etc.), if pressure in a ventricle is greater, the sound will occur later / is protracted. So if RV pressure becomes greater for whatever reason → P2 occurs later → wider splitting. So pulmonary artery hypertension = wide-splitting. If LV pressure becomes greater → A2 occurs later, and can even occur after P2 → paradoxical splitting. So LVH = paradoxical splitting. When R or L ventricular pressure exceeds the pulmonic arterial and aortic pressure, respectively, the valves open. Then the ventricle will lose pressure as blood ejects, followed by isovolumetric relaxation marking the onset of diastole, and the pressure within the ventricle falls below the pressure distal to the valve → valve shuts. Normally splitting oscillates with the respiratory cycle. Inhalation causes P2 to occur later → decrease in intrathoracic pressure → increased venous return to right atrium → more blood in right ventricle → more preload → more pressure → time it takes for RV pressure to fall below pulmonic arterial pressure is greater → P2 will occur slightly later with inhalation. With exhalation it’s the opposite. P2 occurs slightly sooner because increased intrathoracic pressure will attenuate venous return → less preload in RV → less pressure in RV → time it takes for RV pressure to fall below pulmonic arterial pressure is less → pulmonic valve closes slightly sooner → distance between A2 and P2 is less.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is fixed splitting of S2?
rapidFireQAs.a: Super HY for atrial septal defect (ASD) → sometimes can be written as “wide, fixed splitting of S2” → it’s not the “wide” that matters; you need to remember fixed splitting. Wide splitting just means RVH, which can occur due to chronic volume overload in the setting of some ASDs.

rapidFireQAs.q: What does “splitting of S1 mean”?
rapidFireQAs.a: highly unlikely to show up on the USMLE, don’t worry, but for the sake of some people who’d ask, it’s usually seen in right bundle branch block (BBB), which causes delayed closure of the tricuspid valve.

rapidFireQAs.q: Maneuvers that decrease blood in the heart
rapidFireQAs.a: Valsalva; standing up from seated position; sitting up from supine position; administration of nitrates → any of these will cause MVP + HOCM to get worse; all other murmurs will soften or not change.

rapidFireQAs.q: Maneuvers that increase blood in the heart
rapidFireQAs.a: Lying down; leg raise while supine; squatting; hand-grip.

rapidFireQAs.q: How does Valsalva decrease blood in the heart?
rapidFireQAs.a: attempted exhalation against a closed glottis → robust increase in intrathoracic pressure → decreased venous return → decreased cardiac preload.

rapidFireQAs.q: How do nitrates decrease blood in the heart?
rapidFireQAs.a: Increased venodilation + venous pooling → decreased venous return to the right heart → decreased cardiac preload.

rapidFireQAs.q: How does hand-grip increase blood in the heart?
rapidFireQAs.a: hand-grip increases afterload → LV cannot eject blood as readily → greater volume of blood left in the LV; it should be pointed out, however, that it would be incorrect to say hand-grip increases preload, as this effect is indirect.

rapidFireQAs.q: Exceptions regarding handgrip in terms of murmur intensities?
rapidFireQAs.a: decreases intensity of aortic stenosis (same as HOCM) + increases intensity of mitral stenosis (in an NBME vignette).

rapidFireQAs.q: How does respiration relate to left- vs right-sided murmurs?
rapidFireQAs.a: inspiration makes right-sided murmurs worse; exhalation makes left-sided murmurs worse.

rapidFireQAs.q: Why does inspiration make right-sided murmurs worse?
rapidFireQAs.a: inspiration → decreased intrathoracic pressure → easier for blood to return to the RA → increased venous return → more preload in right heart → worsening of TR, TS, PR, PS.

rapidFireQAs.q: Why does inspiration soften left-sided murmurs?
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased intrathoracic pressure → increased pulmonary vascular compliance → transient decrease in pulmonary venous return to the LA → decreased LA preload; it should be noted that although RA preload increases, this effect does not carry over to the LA because of pulmonary vascular pooling.

rapidFireQAs.q: Why does expiration soften right-sided murmurs?
rapidFireQAs.a: expiration → increased intrathoracic pressure → harder for blood to return to the RA → decreased venous return → less preload in right heart → softening of TR, TS, PR, PS.

rapidFireQAs.q: Why does expiration intensify left-sided murmurs?
rapidFireQAs.a: expiration → increased intrathoracic pressure → decreased pulmonary vascular compliance → transient increase in pulmonary venous return to the LA → increased LA preload; it should be noted that although RA preload decreases, this effect does not carry over to the LA because of pulmonary vascular compression.

rapidFireQAs.q: What does VSD sound like?
rapidFireQAs.a: Holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border. Can sometimes be described as having palpable thrill or heave. Q can also mention a diastolic rumble in addition to the holosystolic murmur due to volume reverberations (I've seen it on NBME).

rapidFireQAs.q: If you patch/repair a VSD, what will happen to pressure in the LV, RV, and LA? (up or down arrows)
rapidFireQAs.a: repairing a VSD will cause up LV, down RV, down LA → the down LA always confuses people → repair of VSD means less blood entering RV → less blood going back through the lungs to the LA.

rapidFireQAs.q: Who gets AVSD (atrioventricular septal defect)?
rapidFireQAs.a: Down syndrome (aka endocardial cushion defect).

rapidFireQAs.q: What does ASD sound like and why?
rapidFireQAs.a: as discussed earlier, fixed splitting of S2 → when you’ve got an ASD, blood is constantly moving L –> R from LA –> RA (pressure is always greater on the left side). So the effects of inhalation/exhalation are minimized in terms of the A2-P2 split bc you’ll always have relatively constant LA → RA flow (and resultant steady RA preload) irrespective of inspiration. The sound can also be described as “wide, fixed splitting” bc of increased RV preload → delayed closure of P2 relative to A2 → slight widening, but it’s still fixed for the reasons explained above.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is the fossa ovalis?
rapidFireQAs.a: impression in the interatrial septum following closure of the wall during embryological development. Failure of closure leads to patent foramen ovale, which is a type of ASD.

rapidFireQAs.q: ASD/VSD in relation to blood pO2?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE loves making you guess whether you have an ASD or VSD based on info they give you about blood pO2. If they say pO2 increases from SVC to RA, you know the answer is ASD. If they say pO2 increases from RA to RV, you know VSD is the answer. Path of blood through the heart/lungs (IVC/SVC → RA → RV → pulmonary arteries (deoxygenated) → pulmonary veins (oxygenated) → LA → LV → aorta).

rapidFireQAs.q: What does MVP sound like?
rapidFireQAs.a: as mentioned earlier, mid-systolic click, over 4th intercostal space, left mid-clavicular line.

rapidFireQAs.q: Who gets MVP?
rapidFireQAs.a: most common heart murmur; polygenic; usually benign + incidental; can also get in connective tissue disorders (i.e., Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos).

rapidFireQAs.q: Murmurs seen in connective tissue disorders
rapidFireQAs.a: MVP or AR.

rapidFireQAs.q: What does myxomatous degeneration mean?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = MVP → connective tissue degeneration.

rapidFireQAs.q: What does MR sound like?
rapidFireQAs.a: holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur over 4th intercostal space, left mid-clavicular line; classically radiates to the axilla but by all means doesn’t have to.

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of MR?
rapidFireQAs.a: ischemia; student says “what do you mean?” → atherosclerosis (i.e., due to diabetes, smoking, HTN, familial) → ischemia → structural heart change (LVH + LV dilatation) + papillary muscle weakening → MVP. This is not the same thing as full-blown papillary muscle rupture following an MI; mere ischemia in the absence of MI can cause MR.

rapidFireQAs.q: 68M + T2DM + dilated heart on CXR + S3 heart sound + 2/6 holosystolic murmur over left chest; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: MR due to ischemia from atherosclerosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 68M + T2DM + crushing central chest pain + 3 days later has sudden-onset 4/6 holosystolic murmur over left chest; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: MR from papillary muscle rupture.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + obvious Marfan syndrome in vignette + stethoscope Q where it starts hovering over aortic valve region; what do you do?
rapidFireQAs.a: you’re listening for either AR or MVP, so if you don’t hear anything, just move the stethoscope to the mitral area and you’ll hear the mid-systolic click.

rapidFireQAs.q: What does mitral stenosis sound like?
rapidFireQAs.a: diastolic opening snap with a decrescendo mid-late diastolic murmur.

rapidFireQAs.q: Who gets MS?
rapidFireQAs.a: 99% due to previous rheumatic fever as a kid.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is mechanism for rheumatic fever?
rapidFireQAs.a: type II hypersensitivity against M-protein of Group A Strep (S. pyogenes) → immune system makes antibodies against Group A Strep M-protein that cross-react with the mitral valve (molecular mimicry).

rapidFireQAs.q: How does rheumatic fever present?
rapidFireQAs.a: JONES (J©NES) → Joints (polyarthritis) + © (myocarditis / mitral valve disease) + Nodules (subcutaneous nodules over bony prominences) + Erythema marginatum (appears annular [ring-like] and serpiginous [snake-like]; important vocab words actually for medicine) + Sydenham chorea (antibody-mediated destruction of corpus striatum of basal ganglia) → my biggest advice here is to remember “marginatum” because it’s specifically seen in RF; don’t be that person going around saying “RF has……..erythema multiforme…..?” The latter is usually seen as one of the types of drug rashes.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12F + red tongue + salmon body rash; Dx and Tx?
rapidFireQAs.a: scarlet fever caused by Group A Strep. Must give penicillin to prevent RF.

rapidFireQAs.q: RF caused by cutaneous Group A Strep?
rapidFireQAs.a: No. Cutaneous infections (i.e., impetigo, erysipelas, cellulitis) can cause post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), but not RF. RF is caused by pharyngitis / scarlet fever (pharyngitis + body rash).

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M + Hx of rheumatic fever as a child; what murmur does he most likely have now?
rapidFireQAs.a: MS.

rapidFireQAs.q: 40M + Hx of rheumatic fever as a child + rumbling diastolic murmur; which of the following is most likely part of his Hx as a child?
rapidFireQAs.a: mitral regurgitation. → this is exceedingly HY → RF causes MR acutely in the child but will cause MS later in life as the valve scars over.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12M + fever + sore throat + painful joints + annular skin rash + heart murmur; most likely murmur that he has?
rapidFireQAs.a: MR, not MS.

rapidFireQAs.q: 12M + fever + sore throat + painful joints + annular skin rash + 2/6 holosystolic murmur over left chest; as an adult, what might we expect in this patient?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = diastolic rumbling murmur with opening snap (MS); even though right now he has MR, later in life it will become MS.

rapidFireQAs.q: 33F + pregnant at 20 weeks + new-onset dyspnea + crackles in both lung fields + diastolic rumbling murmur; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: mitral stenosis presenting symptomatically now that plasma volume has increased ~50% in pregnancy.

rapidFireQAs.q: 33F + pregnant at 38 weeks + prominent bilateral ankle pitting edema + dyspnea; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: peripartum dilated cardiomyopathy (antibody-mediated; idiopathic).

rapidFireQAs.q: 33F + pregnant at 32 weeks + mild ankle edema; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: normal edema seen in pregnancy.

rapidFireQAs.q: Does peripartum dilated cardiomyopathy come back in subsequent pregnancies?
rapidFireQAs.a: Yes, and it gets worse.

rapidFireQAs.q: 33F + peripartum dilated cardiomyopathy; best way to predict prognosis if she goes on to have a future pregnancy?
rapidFireQAs.a: TTE (ejection fraction predicts prognosis for future pregnancy).

rapidFireQAs.q: If 99% of MS is due to Hx of rheumatic fever, what else can cause it?
rapidFireQAs.a: Libman-Sacks endocarditis in SLE is associated with MS. 60% of those with LS endocarditis have anti-phospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant).

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + SLE + diastolic rumbling murmur; most likely characteristic of valvular lesion?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = “verrucous vegetations on both sides of the mitral valve” for LS endocarditis.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28M IV drug user + 2/6 holosystolic murmur at left sternal border that increases with inspiration + fever; most likely characteristic of valvular lesion?
rapidFireQAs.a: “large, friable, floppy vegetation” → bacterial endocarditis (tricuspid regurg in this case bc IV drug user).

rapidFireQAs.q: New-onset murmur + fever; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: infective endocarditis (IE) until proven otherwise. Unlike rheumatic fever, this is actual bacterial colonization of a heart valve + production of vegetation; RF is a mere antibody response.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is acute endocarditis?
rapidFireQAs.a: no Hx of valve abnormality; caused almost always by S. aureus; classically seen in IV drug users); classic new-onset murmur + fever presentation.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is subacute endocarditis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Hx of valve abnormality, i.e., congenital defect, Hx of RF; classically occurs following dental procedures; S. viridans (same thing as S. sanguinis or S. mutans) is classic cause; USMLE wants you to know S. viridan’s production of limit dextrins (carbohydrates) enables binding to mitral + aortic valve.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is HACEK?
rapidFireQAs.a: Gram (-) organisms that can cause endocarditis – Hemophilus species, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella kingae – the yield on the USMLE is extremely low so you do not need to memorize these, but I mention them because students occasionally ask about HACEK + the USMLE likes you to know for some magical reason that Eikenella corrodens is associated with human bites, grows white, and has a bleach-like odor.

rapidFireQAs.q: For IE, blood cultures before Abx, or Abx before blood cultures?
rapidFireQAs.a: Always blood cultures (draw three tubes of blood) before giving Abx.

rapidFireQAs.q: Empiric Tx for endocarditis?
rapidFireQAs.a: Gentamicin (aminoglycoside) PLUS either vancomycin or ampicillin/sulbactam. Add rifampin if patient has prosthetic valve.

rapidFireQAs.q: If culture comes back positive for MSSA (not MRSA)?
rapidFireQAs.a: switch to six weeks nafcillin (highly simplified, but the bottom line is if MSSA is confirmed, USMLE answer is you switch to the beta-lactam).

rapidFireQAs.q: Why switch to beta-lactam if MSSA? Why not just stay on vanc?
rapidFireQAs.a: Beta-lactams are way more efficacious than vanc → vanc is actually not a very good drug, but if the organism causing IE is MRSA, it’s first-line.

rapidFireQAs.q: Who gets pulmonic stenosis and what does it sound like?
rapidFireQAs.a: sounds like aortic stenosis (midsystolic murmur) but increases in intensity with inspiration because it’s right-sided; classically seen as part of tetralogy of Fallot in DiGeorge syndrome; also seen classically in Noonan syndrome (USMLE will not ask you about Noonan syndrome).

rapidFireQAs.q: Who gets pulmonic regurg and what does it sound like?
rapidFireQAs.a: sounds like aortic regurg (holodiastolic) but increases with inspiration; rare, but can be seen in endocarditis in IV drug users.

rapidFireQAs.q: Who gets tricuspid regurg and what does it sound like?
rapidFireQAs.a: same as mitral regurg (holosystolic murmur) but gets louder with inspiration; highest yield cause on USMLE is pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonale (these don't cause pulmonic regurg, so sounds a bit weird). Can also be seen in IV drug user endocarditis and carcinoid syndrome.

rapidFireQAs.q: Who gets tricuspid stenosis and what does it sound like?
rapidFireQAs.a: sounds like mitral stenosis presumably (diastolic rumbling murmur, with or without opening snap; but would increase in intensity with inspiration in theory); very rare; I’ve never seen this in any USMLE question.

rapidFireQAs.q: How does isolated left heart failure present?
rapidFireQAs.a: fluid in the lungs (pulmonary edema) +/- pleural effusion; orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND); depending on the etiology of the heart failure, the structure of the heart will take on different characteristics, but the important point about LH failure is fluid in the lungs → also really important you know that pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) is increased in any LH pathology (even if the pressure is within the acceptable range prior to full-blown LH decompensation, the PCWP is still increased relative to the patient’s original baseline in LH pathology).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is PCWP?
rapidFireQAs.a: equal to left atrial pressure; if you stick a catheter through the venous circulation all the way back to the right heart, and then into the pulmonary circulation, and then into a distal pulmonary capillary such that it can’t go any farther, the pressure reverberations are said to best reflect those of the left atrium. The USMLE is obsessed with PCWP; you need to know it is increased not just in cardiogenic shock, but also in LH pathology as I’ve stated above.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is orthopnea?
rapidFireQAs.a: reflective of LH decompensation → requirement to sleep on multiple pillows when supine to prevent fluid buildup in lungs; when supine, there’s greater venous return → greater preload → worsening of dyspnea because the heart cannot handle the volume (i.e., decompensates) because greater O2 demand by the LV with greater preload.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND)?
rapidFireQAs.a: like orthopnea, reflective of LH decompensation → severe dyspnea that occurs while sleeping due to redistribution of fluid into the lungs; unlike orthopnea, does not immediately subside when sitting up.

rapidFireQAs.q: How does isolated right heart failure present?
rapidFireQAs.a: right ventricular hypertrophy (unless tricuspid pathology), jugular venous distension (JVD), peripheral edema, hepatosplenomegaly (late).

rapidFireQAs.q: What’s the most common cause of right heart failure?
rapidFireQAs.a: left heart failure.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is congestive heart failure (CHF)?
rapidFireQAs.a: right heart failure + left heart failure.

rapidFireQAs.q: What causes left heart failure?
rapidFireQAs.a: systemic HTN, ischemia (atherosclerosis), valvular abnormalities.

rapidFireQAs.q: Since left heart failure is the most common cause of right heart failure, what usually causes isolated right heart failure?
rapidFireQAs.a: lung pathology → when you have lung pathology causing RH failure, that’s called cor pulmonale.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Wait, can you explain cor pulmonale a little more. I’ve heard that a lot but don’t really understand it.”
rapidFireQAs.a: when you have a lung condition like COPD, cystic fibrosis, chronic asthma, etc., that leads to RH failure, we call that cor pulmonale. Probably the most important piece of info regarding this condition is that PCWP is normal, which tells you the cause of the RH failure cannot be from LH origin. For instance, if you have a guy with COPD who also has heart disease, if his PCWP is elevated, then we cannot conclude that his right heart failure is a result of the lung disease in isolation because increased PCWP can lead to RH failure.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + 70-pack-year Hx of smoking + JVD + peripheral edema; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cor pulmonale → signs of RH failure in someone who has lung disease.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + 70-pack-year Hx of smoking + systemic HTN + JVD + peripheral edema + has crackles in lungs + dilated heart on CXR; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: congestive heart failure; patient has combo of left and right heart failure signs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25M + cystic fibrosis + JVD + peripheral edema + crackles in lungs; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cor pulmonale → crackles due to CF, not LH failure.

rapidFireQAs.q: If USMLE asks you for the mechanism of cor pulmonale, what’s the answer?
rapidFireQAs.a: pulmonary hypertension → hypoxic vasoconstriction (e.g., in chronic bronchitis, CF) or obliteration of pulmonary parenchyma (emphysema) will cause a backup of blood and pulmonary HTN → increased afterload on RV → starts the process of cor pulmonale (mere pulmonary HTN is not cor pulmonale; there must be RH failure). Can also be due to fibrosis (e.g., CREST or radiation) + loss of lung parenchyma (emphysema).

rapidFireQAs.q: How will USMLE describe pulmonary HTN?
rapidFireQAs.a: Increased pulmonary vascular markings; loud P2; tricuspid regurg. Loud P2 means valve slams shut due to high pressure distal to it. Highest yield cause of tricuspid regurg on USMLE is pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonale..

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + non-smoker + dyspnea + JVD + increased pulmonary vascular markings; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: primary pulmonary hypertension.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is primary pulmonary HTN?
rapidFireQAs.a: mutation in BMPR2 gene leading to narrowing of pulmonary vessels + RH failure.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for pulmonary HTN
rapidFireQAs.a: most patients will respond to dihydropyridine CCBs; if fail, can use agents like bosentan (endothelin-1 receptor antagonist), prostaglandins (i.e., epoprostenol), or sildenafil (yes, Viagra).

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + non-smoker + dyspnea + JVD + increased pulmonary vascular markings; which of the following might describe her condition?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE answer = increased endothelin-1 expression (which makes sense as we know bosentan is a Tx).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) + what are the causes?
rapidFireQAs.a: heart failure with dilatation of the LV cavity + systolic dysfunction with decreased ejection fraction; classic causes are systemic HTN and ischemia (coronary atherosclerosis), but may also be due to ABCD → Alcohol (EtOH directly damages myocardium); Beriberi (wet beriberi seen in thiamine [B1] deficiency; this is not the same as alcoholic cardiomyopathy; it’s coincidental that this also occurs in alcoholics; alcoholics can get DCM and need not be B1 deficient); Cocaine, Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi), Coxsackie B virus; Doxorubicin (Adriamycin); DCM can also be caused by pregnancy (as discussed earlier) and hemochromatosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: How does DCM present?
rapidFireQAs.a: enlarged cardiac silhouette on CXR (dilated heart), lateralized apex beat (dilated heart); sometimes S3 heart sound; fluid in the lungs (pulmonary edema) +/- pleural effusion; can present with orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND).

rapidFireQAs.q: Is HOCM the same thing as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)?
rapidFireQAs.a: Once again, no. HOCM is an AD condition (as discussed earlier). HCM is the diastolic dysfunction of the LV that ensues secondary to increased LV afterload (i.e., from systemic HTN, AS, or HOCM) → the USMLE will often give you an S4 heart sound for HCM.

rapidFireQAs.q: What about restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM)?
rapidFireQAs.a: diastolic dysfunction with failure of the heart to expand; causes are fibrosis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, scleroderma, prior radiation, etc.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the important arrows for systolic dysfunction?
rapidFireQAs.a: Ejection fraction – decreased; LV pressure – increased; LV volume – increased.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the important arrows for diastolic dysfunction?
rapidFireQAs.a: Ejection fraction – normal; LV pressure – increased; LV volume – normal.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Can you explain restrictive cardiomyopathy vs constrictive pericarditis?”
rapidFireQAs.a: both are characterized by diastolic dysfunction (decreased ability of heart to expand), but in RCM this is due to myocardial stiffness / inelasticity, whereas in CP, the etiology is strictly pericardial, with TB being the most common cause of chronic constrictive pericarditis; CP is associated with calcification on CXR in about a third of patients; calcification is not seen in RCM.

rapidFireQAs.q: 22M + stab wound to left chest + JVD + muffled heart sounds + hypotension; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: cardiac tamponade → Beck triad always seen in USMLE Qs = JVD + muffled heart sounds + hypotension; also associated with pulsus paradoxus.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is pulsus paradoxus?
rapidFireQAs.a: drop in BP of >10 mm Hg on inspiration → reflects inability of the heart to fill → seen in cardiac tamponade, severe lung disease (i.e., severe asthma, COPD), and sometimes severe sleep apnea → my observation is students love to focus on miscellaneous causes of PP, but in reality the USMLE primarily tests cardiac tamponade; Qbank might venture down the asthma route once in a blue moon.

rapidFireQAs.q: What’s the difference between pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade?
rapidFireQAs.a: all tamponades are effusions, but not all effusions are tamponades → a tamponade is merely a pericardial effusion that is associated with hemodynamic decompensation (low BP).

rapidFireQAs.q: What determines whether a pericardial effusion becomes a tamponade?
rapidFireQAs.a: acuteness of fluid accumulation → tamponades can be a small volume that accumulates quickly, i.e., from a stab wound or post-MI LV free-wall rupture; whereas we could have, e.g., a slowly accumulating chylous or serosanguinous accumulation in the setting of lymphoma/malignancy that is large volume but does not lead to tamponade.

rapidFireQAs.q: USMLE asks where pericardial fluid is secreted into (Step 1)
rapidFireQAs.a: between the visceral and parietal serous layers → the pericardium = visceral + parietal serous layers + an outer fibrous layer.

rapidFireQAs.q: 6M + strong radial pulses + cold lower extremities; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: coarctation of the aorta; coarctation need not only occur in Turner syndrome.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is pre-ductal vs post-ductal coarctation?
rapidFireQAs.a: if the coarctation occurs proximal to the ductus arteriosus insertion on the descending aortic arch, it’s called pre-ductal; this will be a very sick/cyanotic baby. In contrast, post-ductal will be the answer for a school-age child or adult who merely has BP/pulses that are greater in the upper extremities.

rapidFireQAs.q: Congenital rubella syndrome + cardiovascular defect; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: PDA → continuous machinery-like murmur, pansystolic-pandiastolic, or to-and-fro; can also present with bounding pulses similar to AR.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to close PDA?
rapidFireQAs.a: indomethacin (NSAID).

rapidFireQAs.q: How to keep PDA open?
rapidFireQAs.a: prostaglandin.

rapidFireQAs.q: Kid is cyanotic at birth; before surgery, what should be given?
rapidFireQAs.a: prostaglandin → open PDA can mask and/or mitigate the effects of cyanotic congenital heart disease.

rapidFireQAs.q: Bile acid sequestrants; important info?
rapidFireQAs.a: colestipol, cholestyramine, colesevelam → decrease enterohepatic circulation of bile acids → liver needs to make more → liver pulls cholesterol out of the blood in order to convert it to more bile acids → decreases serum LDL → may slightly increase TGAs → just be aware of their names + mechanism for Step 1 → these drugs do not decrease mortality.

rapidFireQAs.q: Ezetimibe; mechanism?
rapidFireQAs.a: inhibits absorption of cholesterol through the small bowel wall at brush border → does not decrease mortality → just be aware of this drug name + MOA for Step 1.

rapidFireQAs.q: Fibrates; important info?
rapidFireQAs.a: gemfibrozil, fenofibrate → upregulate lipoprotein lipase (LPL) → increases TGA clearance out of blood → answer on the USMLE is TGAs >300 mg/dL; first-line agent to treat severe hyper-TGAs → also upregulates PPAR-alpha, which increases HDL synthesis → cause hepatotoxicity (same as statins), myositis with increased creatine kinase (CK; especially when combined with statins), and cholesterol gallstones (due to inhibition of 7-alpha-hydroxylase, which converts cholesterol to bile acids) → do not decrease mortality.

rapidFireQAs.q: Why is myositis/rhabdomyolysis more likely when fibrates are combined with statins?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE wants “inhibition of P-450 enzymes” as the answer (fibrates inhibit P-450).

rapidFireQAs.q: Statins; mechanism?
rapidFireQAs.a: competitive, reversible inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase → this secondarily causes upregulation of hepatic LDL receptors → both mechanisms decrease serum LDL → statins decrease morality, not because of their LDL-lowering effect (because other drugs do that too), but because they have an antioxidant effect that transcends the cholesterol-lowering effect → USMLE wants you to know that statins increase HMG-CoA mRNA synthesis (compensatory; makes sense, but students get the Q wrong; this is on an NBME); cause hepatotoxicity and myositis/rhabo (the latter especially when combined with fibrates, as said above).

rapidFireQAs.q: Orlistat; MOA
rapidFireQAs.a: pancreatic lipase inhibitor → sometimes used to Tx obesity → can cause fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies + steatorrhea.

rapidFireQAs.q: Evolocumab + alirocumab; MOA?
rapidFireQAs.a: PCSK9 inhibitors → Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 is an enzyme that breaks down LDL receptors → therefore these drugs prevent breakdown of LDL receptors and decrease LDL cholesterol by enabling greater clearance → these are newer agents than statins and are fair game on the USMLE → New England Journal of Medicine study showed they decrease mortality.

rapidFireQAs.q: Digoxin; MOA?
rapidFireQAs.a: inhibits Na/K-ATPase pump → leads to buildup of Na inside the cardiac myocyte → leads to indirect inhibition of Na/Ca-ATPase pump bc the buildup of intracellular Na disfavors the inward movement of Na via this latter pump → therefore Ca doesn’t move out of the cell → increased intracellular Ca → increased inotropy/contractility → also slows HR via Vagal stimulation.

rapidFireQAs.q: Yellow wavy vision + drug OD? Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: digoxin toxicity.

rapidFireQAs.q: How to Tx digoxin toxicity?
rapidFireQAs.a: normalize potassium + give anti-digoxin Fab fragments + give Mg.

rapidFireQAs.q: Electrolyte disturbance causing digoxin toxicity?
rapidFireQAs.a: hypokalemia (digoxin normally binds to extracellular K+ binding site on the cell, so low K+ means more digoxin binding).

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the Ia Na channel blockers?
rapidFireQAs.a: “the Queen Proclaims Diso’s pyramid.” → Quinidine, Procainamide, Disopyramide → you need to know quinidine causes cinchonism (think “quinchonism”), which is tinnitus + headache → procainamide causes DILE (drug-induced lupus erythematosus, with anti-histone antibodies; really HY!) → procainamide is the answer on the USMLE for the drug used to Tx Wolf-Parkinson-White syndrome (delta wave on ECG) → disopyramide is ultra-LY and unlikely to show up, but it’s mentioned in nearly every resource and completes the mnemonic well → the Ia Na channel blockers increase the risk of torsades de pointes (TdP; a sinusoidal ventricular arrhythmia with high chance of progression to VF and death) → they also increase the action potential duration.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the Ib Na channel blockers?
rapidFireQAs.a: “I’d buy Liddy’s Mexican Tacos.” → Lidocaine, Mexiletine, Tocainide → highest yield detail is that they cause “CNS stimulation/depression”; in other words, you’ll get a Q where a patient was started on an anti-arrhythmic and gets, e.g., delirium, and then they’ll ask you for the drug, which will be, e.g., mexiletine → these agents preferentially act on ischemic tissue → Ibs shorten the action potential duration.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the Ic Na channel blockers?
rapidFireQAs.a: Flecainide, Encainide, Propafenone → highest yield detail is that flecainide is the first-line anti-arrhythmic to Tx atrial fibrillation in the absence of structural or coronary artery disease → Ics do not change action potential duration → do not use post-MI.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the type II anti-arrhythmics?
rapidFireQAs.a: beta-blockers → HY mnemonic for agents that antagonize beta-1 only are “A BEAM of beta-blockers” → Atenolol, Bisoprolol, Esmolol, Acebutolol, Metoprolol → metoprolol used largely as rate control for atrial fibrillation + flutter.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the beta-blockers that also act on alpha-receptors?
rapidFireQAs.a: carvedilol + labetalol antagonize both alpha- and beta-receptors.

rapidFireQAs.q: Which beta-blockers decrease mortality in heart failure?
rapidFireQAs.a: nebivolol, carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol XR.

rapidFireQAs.q: Notable use of timolol?
rapidFireQAs.a: topical solution used for glaucoma → decreases aqueous humour production.

rapidFireQAs.q: Notable side-effects of beta-blockers?
rapidFireQAs.a: patients with depression + sexual dysfunction.

rapidFireQAs.q: Contraindications to beta-blockers
rapidFireQAs.a: severe lung disease (asthma w/ Hx of hospitalization or O2 use; COPD); severe or psychotic depression; 2nd or 3rd degree heart block; symptomatic bradycardia; use cautiously in severe diabetes due to masking of hypoglycemic events.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for beta-blocker overdose?
rapidFireQAs.a: glucagon.

rapidFireQAs.q: Important point about BB in relation to pheochromocytoma?
rapidFireQAs.a: Never give beta-blocker before alpha-blocker; always give phenoxybenzamine (irreversible alpha-blocker) before beta-blocker in pheo.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the type III anti-arrhythmics?
rapidFireQAs.a: potassium channel blockers → amiodarone, dronedarone, sotalol, ibutilide, dofetilide → often used in ventricular arrhythmias and in patients being defibrillated unsuccessfully → can be used in atrial fibrillation for rhythm control in those with structural heart disease who cannot take flecainide.

rapidFireQAs.q: Points about amiodarone?
rapidFireQAs.a: causes TdP, pulmonary fibrosis, drug-induced thyroid dysfunction (~40% iodine by weight), corneal deposits, blue-grey skin discoloration → do PFTs, TFTs, LFTs before commencing amiodarone.

rapidFireQAs.q: What are the type IV anti-arrhythmics?
rapidFireQAs.a: non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers → verapamil, diltiazem → verapamil is aka non-dihydropyridine CCB → acts selectively on cardiac (nodal) tissue; in contrast, dihydropyridines like nifedipine act on vascular smooth muscle; diltiazem is said to be a mixed agent → verapamil’s notable use is for AF rate control in patients who cannot receive beta-blockers → verapamil causes constipation (really HY); it can also cause hyperprolactinemia; diltiazem has occasional utility in the Tx of anal fissure and achalasia.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is ivabradine?
rapidFireQAs.a: inhibits myocardial “funny” Na channels (phase IV of AP) → may be attempted in select patients with stable angina who cannot take beta-blockers → can cause “luminous phenomenon,” which is brightness in an area of the visual field.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is sacubitril?
rapidFireQAs.a: neprilysin inhibitor → neprilysin is an enzyme that breaks down ANP and BNP → therefore sacubitril can be used as an antihypertensive to allow the kidney to excrete sodium and water → sacubitril usually used in combination with valsartan as sacubitril/valsartan in the Mx of heart failure (i.e., can be used in place of ACEi or ARB monotherapy during the initial Tx of HF).

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of heart failure?
rapidFireQAs.a: Start with ACEi, ARB, or sacubitril + ACEi/ARB (beta-blocker first is wrong answer on USMLE) → then make sure patient is euvolemic with furosemide → then add beta-blocker (metoprolol XR, bisoprolol, carvedilol, or nebivolol; these four decrease mortality in HF) → if EF still low, add spironolactone → if EF still low, add COMBO of hydralazine + nitrates (combo decreases mortality, especially in African Americans; USMLE Q will mention CHF patient on like 12 meds, and you’ll see hydralazine is one of them, which isn’t typical, and then they’ll ask how the pharm regimen can be modified to decrease morbidity / risk of mortality, and the answer = “add isosorbide ditrate”) → if EF still low, add digoxin → if EF still low, use implantable defibrillator.

rapidFireQAs.q: Super important point about above sequence?
rapidFireQAs.a: Digoxin and furosemide DO NOT decrease mortality (USMLE is obsessed with that point).

rapidFireQAs.q: What is ranolazine?
rapidFireQAs.a: sodium channel blocker used rarely for angina.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism of nitrates?
rapidFireQAs.a: NO activates guanylyl cyclase → increased cGMP production → increased protein kinase G → increased dephosphorylation of myosin light-chain kinase → vascular smooth muscle relaxation → work on veins >> arteries → venodilatation is main effect → must not use with sildenafil (sildenafil inhibits PDE-5 → prevents breakdown of cGMP → severe hypotension with nitrates).

rapidFireQAs.q: What about sodium nitroprusside?
rapidFireQAs.a: works on both arteries and veins → used in hypertensive emergencies → can cause cyanide toxicity → if patient with HTN emergency gets confusion after administration of SN, the answer = cyanide toxicity; if patient has confusion before administration, answer = hypertensive encephalopathy.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is fenoldopam?
rapidFireQAs.a: dopamine 1 (D1) receptor agonist → dilates both renal afferent and efferent arterioles → used to maintain renal perfusion in hypertensive emergency.

rapidFireQAs.q: 66M + back pain + hypercalcemia + renal insufficiency + Q shows you a pic of a white, fibrotic-appearing heart; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = cardiac amyloidosis → seen classically in multiple myeloma (renal insufficiency is often renal amyloidosis).

rapidFireQAs.q: Hypovolemic shock arrows
rapidFireQAs.a: CO down, VR down, TPR up, PCWP down (or normal).

rapidFireQAs.q: Cardiogenic shock arrows
rapidFireQAs.a: CO down, VR down, TPR up, PCWP up.

rapidFireQAs.q: Septic + anaphylactic shock arrows
rapidFireQAs.a: CO up, VR up, TPR down, PCWP normal.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neurogenic shock + adrenal crisis arrows
rapidFireQAs.a: CO down, VR down, TPR down, PCWP normal.

rapidFireQAs.q: “Can you explain ‘autoregulation’?”
rapidFireQAs.a: Carotid sinus baroreceptors (think “sinus pressure”) are stretch-dependent (higher BP = more stretch = more firing of CN IX; lower BP = less stretch = less firing of IX) → so if, for instance, there is high BP, we get increased CN IX (glossopharyngeal) afferent firing to solitary nucleus (nucleus solitarius) of the medulla → result is increased CN X parasympathetic efferent firing to atria (M2 receptors) to slow HR + decreased sympathetic outflow.

rapidFireQAs.q: “I’m still a little confused though. If patient is hypovolemic, then what happens in terms of autoregulation?”
rapidFireQAs.a: decreased stretch of carotid sinus baroreceptors → DECREASED afferent firing of CN IX → decreased efferent CN X firing → decreased ACh binding to M2 receptors at atria + increased sympathetic outflow → HR increases.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mediator that causes cardiac pain?
rapidFireQAs.a: Adenosine. Produced from ATP breakdown. In the setting of ischemia, adenosine builds up, causing cardiac pain.

rapidFireQAs.q: Main regulators of coronary blood flow?
rapidFireQAs.a: O2, CO2, adenosine, NO. But adenosine is most important. Q will tell you norepinephrine was administered, resulting in reduced coronary artery blood flow. Then very soon after blood flow drastically increases. They ask what’s responsible. Answer = adenosine. Presumably NE causes increased oxygen demand, resulting in ATP usage and adenosine production → increased blood flow.

rapidFireQAs.q: Main regulators of skeletal muscle blood flow?
rapidFireQAs.a: “CHALK” → CO2, H+, adenosine, lactate, K+.

rapidFireQAs.q: Q asks if coronary blood flow is greater or equal during systole or diastole when person is at rest vs exercising
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = coronary blood flow is: diastole > systole regardless if patient is at rest or exercising.

rapidFireQAs.q: ST-elevations in leads II, III, aVF; which vessel is affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = posterior descending artery → supplies inferior portion of the heart → sometimes the answer will just be straight-up “right coronary artery” (~70-80% of the time the PDA comes off the RCA).

rapidFireQAs.q: ST-elevations in leads V1, V2, V3; which vessel is affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: left anterior descending artery (LAD; aka anterior interventricular artery) → supplies anterior heart.

rapidFireQAs.q: ST-depressions in leads V1, V2, V3; which vessel is affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: posterior descending artery → posterior infarcts can present as reciprocal ST-depression in the anterior leads.

rapidFireQAs.q: ST-elevations in V4, V5, V6; which vessel is affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: left circumflex artery (LCx) → supplies left lateral heart.

rapidFireQAs.q: Hypokinesis of the apex of the heart on echo; which vessel is affected?
rapidFireQAs.a: LAD → supplies apex.

rapidFireQAs.q: Wide-complex tachycardia
rapidFireQAs.a: ventricular tachycardia (VT).

rapidFireQAs.q: Narrow-complex tachy
rapidFireQAs.a: SVT.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for SVT
rapidFireQAs.a: vagal/carotid massage (“vagal maneuvers”) first; if doesn’t work, then adenosine.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of VT
rapidFireQAs.a: anti-arrhythmics, e.g., amiodarone.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of SVT or VT in setting of coma or low BP
rapidFireQAs.a: direct-current countershock.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of first-degree heart-block or second-degree Mobitz I (Wenckebach)
rapidFireQAs.a: observe.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx of second-degree Mobitz II or third-degree heart block
rapidFireQAs.a: pacemaker.

rapidFireQAs.q: First-degree heart-block
rapidFireQAs.a: PR-interval >200 milliseconds.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mobitz I
rapidFireQAs.a: gradually prolonging PR-interval before a QRS drops.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mobitz II
rapidFireQAs.a: no gradual prolongation of PR-interval; QRS randomly drops.

rapidFireQAs.q: Third-degree
rapidFireQAs.a: HR super slow at 30-40; no relation between p-waves and QRS complexes.

rapidFireQAs.q: Infective causes of third-degree
rapidFireQAs.a: Lyme disease, congenital lupus, diphtheria.

rapidFireQAs.q: Mechanism of Goodpasture syndrome?
rapidFireQAs.a: antibodies against type IV collagen → “2, 3, 4… 2, 3, 4… 2, 3, 4. The Goodpasture is marching in the field, 2, 3, 4!”→ Type 2 hypersensitivity against the alpha-3 chains of type 4 collagen. Presents as male 20s-40s with hemoptysis + hematuria.

rapidFireQAs.q: Hematuria + hemoptysis + “head-itis” (mastoiditis, sinusitis, otitis, nasal septal perforation)
rapidFireQAs.a: Wegener granulomatosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Annoying new name for Wegener
rapidFireQAs.a: granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of Wegener
rapidFireQAs.a: c-ANCA (anti-PR3; anti-proteinase 3).

rapidFireQAs.q: Asthma + eosinophilia
rapidFireQAs.a: Churg-Strauss.

rapidFireQAs.q: Annoying new name for CS
rapidFireQAs.a: eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of CS
rapidFireQAs.a: p-ANCA (anti-MPO; anti-myeloperoxidase).

rapidFireQAs.q: Hematuria in isolation + p-ANCA in serum
rapidFireQAs.a: microscopic polyangiitis (MP).

rapidFireQAs.q: Severe renal disease in Wegener or Goodpasture or MP
rapidFireQAs.a: rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (crescentic).

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + hematuria + hemoptysis
rapidFireQAs.a: Goodpasture syndrome.

rapidFireQAs.q: 44M + hematuria + hemopytisis + head-itis
rapidFireQAs.a: Wegener.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is polyarteritis nodosa
rapidFireQAs.a: medium-vessel vasculitis characterized by immune complex deposition in vascular walls + fibrinoid necrosis (can be described as “segmental, ischemic necrosis”).

rapidFireQAs.q: Polyarteritis nodosa is associated with what infection?
rapidFireQAs.a: 30% of patients are HepB positive.

rapidFireQAs.q: What do you see on renal artery angiogram in PN
rapidFireQAs.a: “beads on a string” (similar to fibromuscular dysplasia, although completely unrelated diseases).

rapidFireQAs.q: Kid jumps into cold lake; what happens to (arrows) central blood volume, ADH, and ANP levels?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = central blood volume increases, ADH decreases, ANP increases → cold means increased alpha-1 agonism in arterioles to constrict distally to retain heat → increased blood volume in larger vessels → increased right atrial filling + stretch → increased ANP release; increased central blood volume also increases baroreceptor activity at carotid sinus → not only leads to increased activity of the autoregulation CN IX/X loop, but also suppresses ADH release to decrease free water reabsorption in the medullary collecting duct of the kidney. If this part sounds confusing, you can remember the soccer-mom explanation instead, which is just: if you have more volume in your core, your body "thinks" it doesn't want more volume, so ADH goes down to decrease free water reabsorption in the kidneys.

rapidFireQAs.q: Medial malleolus ulcer + hyperpigmentation of lower legs; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic venous insufficiency

rapidFireQAs.q: Punched-out ulcer on foot + intermittent claudication; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: arterial insufficiency (peripheral vascular disease)

rapidFireQAs.q: What causes venous insufficiency?
rapidFireQAs.a: valvular incompetence (most commonly familial), resulting in venous reflux + insufficiency. Patient need not have varicose veins. Venous insufficiency can present as hyperpigmentation due to hemosiderin deposition and Hx of DVT.

rapidFireQAs.q: What causes arterial insufficiency
rapidFireQAs.a: atherosclerosis (diabetes, followed by smoking, are the two most acceleratory risk factors; hypertension is the most common risk factor)

rapidFireQAs.q: Varicose veins and venous insufficiency same thing?
rapidFireQAs.a: varicose veins are one of the mere presentations of venous insufficiency, so yes, patients with varicose veins have venous insufficiency.

rapidFireQAs.q: Tx for arterial insufficiency
rapidFireQAs.a: exercise regimen first, THEN cilostazol (phosphodiesterase 3 inhibitor)

rapidFireQAs.q: What must you do before starting the exercise regimen in the Tx of arterial insufficiency
rapidFireQAs.a: ECG stress test to ascertain patient’s exercise tolerance.

rapidFireQAs.q: What if patient has abnormal baseline ECG (e.g., BBB)
rapidFireQAs.a: do echo stress test instead.

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient with CVD is on various medications + has hyperkalemia; why?
rapidFireQAs.a: ACEi, ARB, and spironolactone all can cause hyperkalemia.

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient with CVD is on various medications + hypokalemia; why?
rapidFireQAs.a: furosemide (Loop diuretic)

rapidFireQAs.q: When do we start patients on furosemide?
rapidFireQAs.a: to fluid unload (dyspnea in heart failure or peripheral edema)

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient is started on furosemide + still has fluid overload; what’s the next diuretic to use
rapidFireQAs.a: spironolactone → essentially furosemide causes increased K wasting, so we must give a potassium-sparing diuretic to balance the effect (spironolactone).

rapidFireQAs.q: What’s the MOA of spironolactone
rapidFireQAs.a: aldosterone receptor antagonist.

rapidFireQAs.q: Side-effects of spironolactone
rapidFireQAs.a: hyperkalemia; gynecomastia.

rapidFireQAs.q: When do we give patients spironolactone apart from as a step-up from Loops?
rapidFireQAs.a: added onto heart failure management after a patient is already on ACEi (or ARB) + beta-blocker. In other words, for heart failure: give ACEi (or ARB) first, then add beta-blocker, then add spironolactone.

rapidFireQAs.q: Major side-effects of beta-blockers
rapidFireQAs.a: depression + sexual dysfunction (avoid in these patients)

rapidFireQAs.q: Major side-effect of naproxen
rapidFireQAs.a: fluid retention (edema) due to increased renal retention of sodium.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is naproxen?
rapidFireQAs.a: NSAID that the USMLE is obsessed with for some reason.

rapidFireQAs.q: Why might NSAIDs cause fluid retention / renal retention of sodium?
rapidFireQAs.a: knocking out COX → decreased prostaglandin synthesis → decreased renal afferent arteriolar dilatation → decreased renal blood flow → PCT of kidney compensates for perceived low blood volume by increasing Na reabsorption → water follows sodium → edema.

rapidFireQAs.q: Most common cause of carotid plaques?
rapidFireQAs.a: HTN → the strong systolic impulse from the heart pounds the carotids --> endothelial damage --> atherosclerosis.

rapidFireQAs.q: What % of people over age 80 have AF?
rapidFireQAs.a: 8% of people over age 80 have AF, which is why age is a huge risk factor. In other words, if the vignette says the guy is 58, AF is probably less likely just based on shear probability, regardless of hypertensive status." And, once again, knowing that AF is often paroxysmal is really important.

rapidFireQAs.q: High-Yield Pearl #267
rapidFireQAs.a: For the actual Tx of the AF, we do rate control before rhythm control (the management is actually heavily involved, but for the USMLE know the following): o Rate control: beta-blocker first-line (metoprolol). If beta-blocker avoided (i.e., severe or psychotic depression, sexual dysfunction, COPD, Hx of asthma requiring oxygen or hospitalization, 2nd/3rd-degree heart block), verapamil is the next choice. If rate control fails, go to rhythm control. o Rhythm control: Flecainide (type-Ic Na channel blocker) first-line in those without any structural (i.e., LVH or valvular problems) or coronary artery disease (any symptomatology of CVD or PVD means patient has coronary artery disease). In those who cannot receive flecainide, other anti-arrhythmics like amiodarone, dronedarone, and dofetilide may be used.

rapidFireQAs.q: 68F + diabetic + diffuse, dull abdo pain 1-2 hours after meals; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic mesenteric ischemia due to atherosclerosis of SMA or IMA, not duodenal ulcer (if they want the latter, they’ll say 29M from Indonesia) → essentially stable angina of the bowel.

rapidFireQAs.q: 68F + Hx of intermittent claudication + CABG + abdo pain 1-2 hours after eating meals; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: chronic mesenteric ischemia.

rapidFireQAs.q: 78M + Hx of AF + acute-onset severe abdo pain “out of proportion to physical exam”; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: acute mesenteric ischemia due to embolus (LA mural thrombus that’s launched off to SMA or IMA).

rapidFireQAs.q: 66F + has episode of ventricular fibrillation + defibrillated + now has severe abdo pain; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: acute mesenteric ischemia → defibrillation likely launched off LA mural thrombus the patient had (even if no overt Afib).

rapidFireQAs.q: 68F + diabetic + Hx of diffuse, dull abdo pain 1-2 hours after meals + now has 2-day Hx of severe abdo pain out of proportion to physical exam; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: acute on chronic mesenteric ischemia due to ruptured atherosclerotic plaque (akin to an “MI” of the bowel).

rapidFireQAs.q: Dx of acute + chronic mesenteric ischemia?
rapidFireQAs.a: USMLE answer = mesenteric angiography.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45M + has FHx of DCM + cirrhosis + generalized hyperpigmentation; his heart may show accumulation of what?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = Iron. Diagnosis is hereditary hemochromatosis, which can present as “bronze diabetes” → 1) increased glucose levels + 2) hyperpigmentation + 3) other miscellaneous finding like cardiomyopathy, or pseudogout, or infertility.

rapidFireQAs.q: 92F dies in her sleep; heart is most likely to show what on biopsy?
rapidFireQAs.a: lipofuscin → yellow-brown “age pigment” that reflects autodigestion of intracellular lipid residues by lysosomal enzymes.

rapidFireQAs.q: Post-MI dyspnea; mechanism for fluid in lungs?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = “increased pulmonary capillary pressure” → the wrong answer is “increased permeability of pulmonary capillaries.” The former refers to transudate; the latter refers to exudate.

rapidFireQAs.q: Left dominant coronary circulation in someone with STEMI in leads II, III, and aVF; what is the pathway of vessels here?
rapidFireQAs.a: firstly, need to identify this as inferior infarct; then identify that the posterior descending artery (PDA) supplies the inferior portion of the heart; Q gives you “LCA,” “LCx” and “PDA” as answers in different order; answer = LCA → LCx → PDA (left-dominant means must start with LCA; we know PDA finishes the supply, so LCx must be in the middle).

rapidFireQAs.q: Patient has end-systolic volume of 100 mL + end-diastolic volume is 150 mL; what’s the ejection fraction in terms of %?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = (EDV – ESV / EDV) = (150 – 100 / 150) = 50/150 = 33.3% → USMLE will ask you to calculate.

rapidFireQAs.q: What is normal ejection fraction?
When might the Q say the EF is high?
rapidFireQAs.a: sometimes in high-output cardiac failure due to AV shunts, i.e., in Paget disease of bone, hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (pulmonary AVM), or patient with previous dialysis + shunt.

rapidFireQAs.q: 29F + SOB with exertion + S3 heart sound + laterally displaced apex beat + CXR shows cardiomegaly + Kerley B lines + TTE shows EF of 30%; Dx?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = CHF → you’re supposed to say, “Wait, in a young patient without any specific disorder? And they don’t mention pregnancy either?” → but the rest of the presentation is overwhelming, so you need to know this is ultra-classic / HY for CHF.

rapidFireQAs.q: NBME Q on CHF asks for (up or down) for LV stroke volume, LA pressure, and TPR
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = LV stroke volume down; LA pressure up; TPR up.

rapidFireQAs.q: 56M + MI + has coronary angioplasty to restore blood flow + now has idioventricular arrhythmia; why?
rapidFireQAs.a: answer = “generation of reactive oxygen species”; this refers to reperfusion injury.

rapidFireQAs.q: 32F + abdominal bruit + BP of 160/100. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑ or ↓) for Na+, K+, pH, bicarb, and CO2?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↑ Na+ , ↓ K+ , ↑ pH, ↑ bicarb, ↑ CO2. — Diagnosis is fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD), which is tunica media proliferation, generally in women 20s-50s. This results in decreased renal perfusion → renin secretion by JGC → RAAS activation. • This is not the same as renal artery stenosis, which is due to atherosclerosis. The vignette will instead be a patient with, e.g., intermittent claudication, Hx of CABG, or many years of smoking.

rapidFireQAs.q: 25F + goes for a 10-mile run + has not yet had anything to drink. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for carotid sinus baroreceptor firing rate, vagus nerve firing rate, and sinoatrial sympathetic activity?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ Carotid sinus baroreceptor firing rate, ↓ vagus nerve firing rate, ↑ sinoatrial sympathetic activity. — The feedback loop for autoregulation is: • Carotid sinus baroreceptors (sense blood pressure/volume) → afferent cranial nerve IX (glossopharyngeal) to solitary nucleus of the medulla → efferent CN X (vagus; parasympathetic) to cardiac nodal tissue → change in heart rate accordingly. • Patient is dehydrated. The carotid sinus baroreceptor firing rate is stretch-dependent, meaning that if blood volume (or BP) is low, firing rate is low, not high. Students frequently get this wrong because they think that any change in pressure – high or low – “wakes up” the baroreceptors and they always fire more, but this is not the case. High BP = high firing rate; low BP or dehydration = low firing rate. • If BP low → carotid sinus stretch low → CN IX activity low → CN X activity low → HR goes up. • If BP high → carotid sinus stretch high → CN IX activity high → CN X activity high → HR goes down. • If you have trouble with this, just remember that BP, CN IX, and CN X activity go the same direction. • Sympathetic activity goes the opposite direction. • If BP low → low CN IX firing rate → high sympathetic firing rate → HR goes up. • The afferent CN IX / carotid sinus baroreceptor activity arrow being down, not up, in the setting of low BP, is exceedingly HY for USMLE. As I said, many students that up.

As I said, many students that up.

rapidFireQAs.q: 28F + non-smoker + 6-month Hx of progressive shortness of breath + chest x-ray shows increased pulmonary vascular markings + dilated pulmonary artery; there is loud P2 on physical exam. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for PCWP, endothelin-1, pulmonary vascular resistance, and systemic vascular resistance?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↔ PCWP, ↑ endothelin-1, ↑ pulmonary vascular resistance, ↔ systemic vascular resistance. — Diagnosis is primary pulmonary hypertension, usually caused by mutations in BMPR2. • Vignette will usually be a female in her 20s-30s who’s a non-smoker. • Loud P2 means pulmonary hypertension on USMLE. The pulmonary valve is slamming shut because of increased pressure distal to it. • PCWP is normal because the left heart is completely normal. PCWP = LAP. This question 100% tests whether you understand PCWP. PCWP is only high in left heart problems. • Endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor. In pulmonary hypertension, endothelin-1 activity is increased and nitric oxide synthase activity is decreased. Bosentan is an endothelin-1 receptor antagonist used for pulmonary hypertension. • Pulmonary vascular resistance is up because we have constriction of the pulmonary vessels due to increased endothelin-1. • Systemic vascular resistance (i.e., of the peripheral arterioles) is unchanged because this condition only affects the lungs.

rapidFireQAs.q: 45F + type II diabetes mellitus + commenced on enalapril. As a result of this medication, what are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for change in systemic vascular resistance, renal efferent arteriolar diameter, heart rate, and ejection fraction?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ Systemic vascular resistance, ↑ renal efferent arteriolar diameter, ↑ heart rate, ↑ ejection fraction. — Enalapril is an ACE inhibitor. Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor. ACEi will cause decreased vasoconstriction of peripheral arterioles, thereby decreasing blood pressure. • AT II constricts the efferent arterioles. Therefore, giving an ACEi decreases this constrictive effect and increases diameter. • Since systemic vascular resistance decreases, heart rate goes up to compensate via the baroreceptor reflex. o If we dilate arterioles → BP goes down → HR goes up to compensate. o If we constrict arterioles → BP goes up → HR goes down to compensate. • Drugs like ACEi, ARBs (e.g., valsartan), dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (e.g., nifedipine), a1 antagonists (e.g., prazosin), and hydralazine will increase arteriolar diameter → BP goes down → HR goes up to compensate. • Drugs like a1 agonists (phenylephrine, oxymetazoline, midodrine) constrict arterioles → BP goes up → HR goes down to compensate. • Ejection fraction goes up when arteriolar diameter increases because there’s less afterload on the heart → easier for heart to pump. ACEi/ARBs are first-line for heart failure and increase ejection fraction.

rapidFireQAs.q: Neonate + ventricular septal defect (VSD) + has VSD repaired with a prosthetic patch. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for the change in left ventricular pressure, right ventricular pressure, and left atrial pressure as a result of this repair?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↑ Left ventricular pressure, ↓ right ventricular pressure, ↓ left atrial pressure. — When a VSD is repaired, less blood is leaving the left ventricle for the right ventricle, so left ventricular pressure increases and right ventricular pressure decreases. • Since less blood enters the right ventricle, less blood will be returned through the lungs back to the left atrium, thereby decreasing left atrial preload and pressure. • This combo of arrows is on the NBME for Step 1, both on offline and online forms (i.e., the Q is repeated).

rapidFireQAs.q: 4M + holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border. A ventricular septal defect (VSD) and left atrial dilatation are seen on echo. Compared to normal values, what are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for superior vena cava pO2, right atrial pO2, right ventricular pO2, left ventricular pO2, and pulmonary artery pO2?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↔ Superior vena cava pO2, ↔ right atrial pO2, ↑ right ventricular pO2, ↔ left ventricular pO2, pulmonary artery pO2. — The diagnosis is VSD. It is classically described as a holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border. • The left-to-right shunt causes increased preload in the right ventricle, leading to increased circulation back through the lungs to the left atrium, causing left atrial dilatation in some patients. I have seen this on NBME. • The vena cava and RA pO2 are normal because they are proximal to the defect. • Left ventricular pO2 is normal because blood is only moving left to right from high → low pressure.

rapidFireQAs.q: 24M + healthy + changes position from supine to standing up. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for the change in venous return, carotid sinus baroreceptor activity, and cerebral blood flow?
rapidFireQAs.a: ↓ Venous return, ↓ carotid sinus baroreceptor activity, ↓ cerebral blood flow. — Moving from supine to standing / sitting up decreases venous return (due to increased venous pooling). • This means less central blood volume and less cardiac output. • Less cardiac output means less carotid sinus baroreceptor firing rate (i.e., less CN IX afferent firing). • Remember that the carotid sinus baroreceptor firing rate is stretch-dependent. If volume/BP is low, firing rate is low, not high. Likewise, if volume/BP is high, firing rate is high. • Cerebral blood flow is lower because cardiac output is lower.
